---
order: 5
node: AC9S7U04 n5
woven: [AC9S7I04, AC9S7I05]
unit: forces
title: Same push, different mass
summary: "For the same unbalanced force, a heavier object accelerates less than a lighter one. For the same mass, a bigger unbalanced force gives a bigger acceleration. Data from a force investigation show the pattern: acceleration goes up with force and down with mass."
language: science
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8294
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8294/index.html
  readySelector: "#gpanel"
  layout: full
hook: "A rugby front-rower and a winger sprint off the same line with the same push from the ground. Who gets going faster, and why?"
---
You know an unbalanced force changes how something moves, and now you can see what the mass of the thing does to the result.

## Engage: the trolley

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students say the heavier object accelerates more because it has more 'stuff', or that mass makes no difference. The pattern is that mass resists change in motion."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "You give an empty trolley and a full trolley exactly the same steady push. Which one speeds up more?"
  options: ["The empty one: a smaller mass accelerates more for the same force", "The full one: it has more mass to push", "They speed up equally", "Neither: a steady push only gives a steady speed"]
  actual: "The empty one. For the same unbalanced force, a bigger mass means a smaller acceleration. Mass resists changes in motion."
```

## Explore: load the trolley

```step
stage: run
insight: "Changing only the mass, then only the force, and reading the acceleration each time is the controlled investigation the node's data analysis comes from."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#trolley", height: 640 }
tasks:
  - starter: "boards.yml#trolley"
    check: { type: board, text: "The push is 6 N. Set the mass to 2 kg and read the acceleration.", when: "m = 2 and a = 3" }
  - starter: "boards.yml#trolley"
    check: { type: board, text: "Double the mass to 4 kg. What happens to the acceleration?", when: "m = 4 and a = 1.5" }
```

## Explain: the pattern

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Stating the relationship in words, predicting which object accelerates more, and reading the pattern from two data tables meets the three success criteria."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "The same unbalanced force acts on a 2 kg object and an 8 kg object. Which accelerates more?"
      options: ["The 2 kg object", "The 8 kg object", "Both the same"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "More mass means more resistance to a change in motion, so the mass does make a difference.", "On the board, doubling the mass from 2 kg to 4 kg halved the acceleration, so mass matters."]
      explain: "For the same force, the smaller mass accelerates more."
    hint: ["Which would be easier to get moving with the same push, a small trolley or a loaded one?", "Look back at what happened to the acceleration when you doubled the mass on the board."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which statement is right?"
      options: ["A bigger unbalanced force gives a bigger acceleration, and a bigger mass gives a smaller one", "A bigger mass gives a bigger acceleration", "Force and mass don't affect acceleration"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It works the other way round for mass.", "On the board, changing the mass changed the acceleration, and changing the push does too, so both matter."]
      explain: "A bigger force gives more acceleration, but a bigger mass gives less."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "Same trolley, 2 kg. Pushing with 2 N gives 1 m/s², 4 N gives 2 m/s², 6 N gives 3 m/s². What acceleration would 10 N give (m/s²)?"
      answer: 5
      explain: "The acceleration goes up by the same amount for each extra newton, so 10 N gives 5 m/s²."
    hint: ["Look at how much the acceleration goes up each time the push goes up by 2 N.", "Then think about how many steps like that it is from 6 N to 10 N."]
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "Same push of 8 N. A 1 kg trolley accelerates at 8 m/s², 2 kg at 4 m/s², 4 kg at 2 m/s². What acceleration would 8 kg give (m/s²)?"
      answer: 1
      explain: "Each time the mass doubles, the acceleration halves, so 8 kg gives 1 m/s²."
    hint: ["What happens to the acceleration each time the mass goes up?", "Check your idea against the 1 kg to 2 kg step and the 2 kg to 4 kg step, and see if it holds for both."]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can say how force and mass affect acceleration, and read the pattern from data." }
```

## Mix it up

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Acceleration needs an unbalanced force, so the effect of a net force on motion comes back before force and mass are compared."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Looking back at unbalanced forces: a box slides to the right. Friction acts on it towards the left with 6 N and nothing pushes it. What does the box do?"
  options: ["It slows down", "It keeps sliding at a steady speed", "It speeds up to the right", "It stops straight away"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "A steady speed needs balanced forces, but here nothing balances the friction.", "The net force points left, against the motion, so the box can't be speeding up to the right.", "The net force changes the speed gradually, so the box slows down first."]
  explain: "The net force is 6 N to the left, against the motion, so the box slows down."
```

## Elaborate: hit a target

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Choosing the force to hit a target acceleration for a given mass uses the pattern in reverse."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#adjust", height: 640 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "The trolley is 5 kg. Set the push so the acceleration is 2 m/s².", when: "m = 5 and a = 2" }
    hint: ["If the acceleration comes out too small, will you want more push or less?", "Slide the push and read the acceleration under the board each time, until it lands where you want it."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You change the mass to 10 kg and keep the same push. What must happen to the acceleration?"
      options: ["It halves", "It doubles", "It stays the same"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "More mass means less acceleration, not more.", "The push is the same, but now there's twice as much mass to speed up."]
      explain: "For the same push, doubling the mass halves the acceleration."
    hint: "Think about what happened to the acceleration when you doubled the mass from 2 kg to 4 kg."
```

## Elaborate: rockets and roads

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Engineers use the same pattern: to accelerate faster, raise the force or cut the mass."
check:
  type: question
  q: "A rocket burns fuel, so its mass falls while the thrust stays the same. What happens to its acceleration?"
  options: ["It increases", "It decreases", "It stays the same"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Less mass actually means more acceleration.", "The mass changes, so the acceleration changes with it."]
  explain: "The same force on a smaller mass gives a bigger acceleration, and that's one reason rockets are built in stages that fall away."
hint: "Think about the loaded and empty trolleys, and which way a rocket's mass is going as it burns fuel."
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the trolleys with what the board showed." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- For the **same unbalanced force**, a **larger mass** gives a **smaller acceleration**.
- For the **same mass**, a **larger unbalanced force** gives a **larger acceleration**.
- Data show the pattern: acceleration rises with force and falls as mass rises.

```teacher
summary: Students state the qualitative relationship between force, mass and
  acceleration, predict which object accelerates more under the same force, and
  read the pattern from data (AC9S7U04, node 5, an integration node).
time: 17
timing: Engage and Explore 6 min · Explain 8 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical adds
  3 min, Wider about 1 min
goals:
  - I can say what happens to acceleration when the force or the mass changes.
  - I can predict which of two objects accelerates more under the same force.
  - I can read a pattern from force data.
before: >
  A short integration tutorial that follows the four Year 7 forces lessons. Set
  the width with `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or `wider`. The Year 10
  lessons put numbers on this (F = ma); here the aim is the qualitative pattern
  and the data.


  Board notes: the trolley sits on a frictionless track; the board shows the
  acceleration before Play. The data tables in the questions are small, rounded
  numbers chosen for a clear pattern. Don't call the pattern F = ma yet.
running:
  - "Engage: tally the predictions. Ask the 'full one' group what a heavier
    trolley resists."
  - "Explore: ask what happened to the acceleration when the mass doubled."
  - "Explain: the two statements and the data patterns are the success criteria."
  - "In your own words: the two bar graphs and a sentence for each."
struggle: Putting force and mass together. When a student says a heavier object
  accelerates more, ask which one they would rather push to get moving.
stuck:
  - see: A student says acceleration is the same speed.
    ask: Is acceleration how fast, or how quickly speed changes?
    fix: How quickly speed changes. Same force on a bigger mass changes speed more
      slowly.
  - see: A student says heavier means more acceleration.
    ask: Which trolley is easier to get moving?
    fix: The lighter one. Heavier means more resistance to changing motion.
stretch: A 4 kg trolley and a 1 kg trolley are pushed with the same force and
  the 4 kg one accelerates at 2 m/s². How fast does the 1 kg one accelerate? (8
  m/s².)
support: Give the data as two small tables with the acceleration column blank
  for the last row, and ask students to say 'doubles' or 'halves' for each step.
leads: >
  Next: Year 8 energy, then Year 10 Newton's laws, where the pattern becomes F =
  ma.


  In class: a dynamics trolley on a ramp with a light string and different
  masses; a bowling ball and a tennis ball given the same push; data logging
  with light gates if available.
exit:
  q: The same push is given to a 3 kg box and a 6 kg box. Which accelerates more,
    and by how much compared with the other?
  a: The 3 kg box. It accelerates twice as much, because it has half the mass.
explain: >
  For the **same unbalanced force**, a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration.
  For the **same mass**, a larger unbalanced force gives a larger acceleration.
```
